title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We report the exact McNemar result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, present the bootstrap CI as a secondary descriptive summary, explicitly label a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) as exploratory/post‑hoc (it was not specified in the frozen preregistration), and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, high baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations promises reduced manual effort but raises safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that affect code and configuration generation, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates purely downstream validator/repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our precise research question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics), to what degree can a downstream deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes compared with reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally isolates downstream interventions (validation and at‑most‑one repair) so that any paired difference is attributable to those downstream mechanisms rather than to first‑pass generation differences such as prompt engineering, constrained decoding, or sampling variance.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired experiment (Npairs = 1000) with deterministic task selection from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus and archived validator traces. (2) Full execution accounting and preregistration transparency, including an explicit statement that execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). (3) An artifact‑grounded presentation of the preregistered primary inferential outcome (exact two‑sided McNemar) and preregistered descriptive summaries, with explicit labeling of exploratory/post‑hoc analyses.
sections.related_work:
LLM behavior on structured outputs shows frequent hallucinations and high prompt sensitivity that degrade correctness for generated code and configurations; surveys and empirical studies document these issues and motivate verifier/repair architectures [1],[2]. Constrained decoding and schema‑aware planning have been shown to reduce syntactic and executable errors in structured domains, though many demonstrations are outside NetOps and thus depend on validator fidelity when transferred to networking [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI papers present verifier‑assisted repair prototypes, protocol‑mediated governance proposals, and digital‑twin validation concepts that emphasize validator coverage and governance as determinants of operational reliability rather than any single model's output alone [4],[5],[6].

Our study complements these works by preregistering a paired estimand that isolates downstream validation and at‑most‑one repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics, thereby avoiding conflation with first‑pass generation differences. This focused design clarifies what can and cannot be concluded about validator/repair efficacy from paired comparisons that reuse the same initial candidate across conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design fidelity. The preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was frozen before any hosted‑model invocation; its SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest. Key preregistered choices: paired binary design with task_count = 1000 from challenging_workflow_stress_v1; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and sensitivity analyses for missingness.

Shared_initial_candidate interpretive consequences. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics both baseline and guarded episodes begin from the very same sampled candidate; only deterministic validation decisions and the single permitted repair call can create paired differences. Therefore this experiment measures the incremental effect of downstream validator/repair layers only. Any claims about the benefits of constrained decoding, prompt templates, or independent first‑pass guarded prompts would require separately executed arms and are not supported by this paired design.

Execution and validator. The declared runtime configuration recorded the model identifier and provider as gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses); execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset (explicitly not evidence of deterministic sampling). Validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5, which enforces task‑manifest workflow policies (required command sequences, protected fields, and order constraints) via a digital‑twin emulator and returns a deterministic binary safe‑deploy verdict per episode. Retries and missingness treatments were limited and prespecified in the preregistration.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑grounded). The preregistered run completed the planned paired episodes and produced full validator traces and model‑call accounting archived with the run. The provider audit shows the adapter performed one shared initial generation per task and invoked repair on a small number of episodes; these artifacts document that paired differences could only arise from validator/repair activity.

Primary paired outcomes and preregistered inferential test. The preregistered 2×2 paired contingency table is n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625 and therefore does not meet the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05 threshold; preregistered H1 is not supported.

Preregistered secondary descriptive summaries. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]; this bootstrap summary was specified as descriptive. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred; representative archived traces show repairs addressed ordering/sequence violations and the validator accepted repaired candidates after revalidation. No contamination flags, exclusions, or failed episodes were recorded in the archived missingness summary.

Inferential hierarchy (preregistered vs exploratory). The exact two‑sided McNemar is the preregistered confirmatory analysis; its p = 0.0625 is the primary inferential outcome and is not significant at two‑sided α = 0.05. The paired bootstrap CI and a one‑sided McNemar (computed post‑hoc with p = 0.03125) are reported as descriptive or exploratory only; the one‑sided test was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration and therefore does not alter the preregistered confirmatory conclusion. The bootstrap CI excludes zero because percentile bootstrap behavior with extremely sparse discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0) can yield nonzero percentile bounds; this phenomenon is a sampling‑mechanics artifact and does not override the preregistered exact McNemar confirmatory result.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation in context of preregistration and power assumptions. The preregistered power plan targeted a much larger absolute effect under an assumed baseline ≈ 0.60. The observed baseline success rate (0.995) is far higher than planned and therefore produces very few discordant pairs, reducing the paired test's sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch between planned and observed baseline regimes explains why the confirmatory McNemar test was not significant even though the bootstrap CI (descriptive) excludes zero.

Mechanistic implications under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because both arms reused the same sampled initial candidate, only deterministic validator decisions and the single allowed repair could affect paired outcomes. The five observed repairs demonstrate that validator‑triggered repair can avert specific unsafe order/constraint violations in this synthetic corpus. However, the low repair count constrains generalization about repair efficacy across diverse failure modes, and the single‑model, synthetic‑corpus scope limits external validity.

Threats to validity. Construct validity depends on validator coverage: omitted policy checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity is supported by deterministic seeding and complete episode accounting. External validity is limited by single‑model evaluation and a synthetic corpus; further work should vary generator semantics, repair budget, validator rule sets, and model families.
sections.conclusion:
In a preregistered paired study that held the initial sampled candidate constant across conditions, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) over a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked. These artifact‑grounded findings show that downstream validator/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflow settings, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. Full preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run to support reproducibility and preregistered follow‑ups.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
